source.title: Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models
source.authors: Thomas Winninger; B. Addad; Katarzyna Kapusta

record.file_problem: None; full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Computes harmful-minus-harmless refusal directions and tests activation steering with them; it also optimizes suffixes to mimic direction suppression and measures jailbreak success.
record.gate_note: The paper reports probe accuracy and direction/cosine analyses, but these do not directly measure refusal behavior and are not rows here. Steering-SSR is tested through jailbreak success rates. The cross-model transfer table concerns transfer of optimized suffixes, not transfer of the direction itself. No weight-edit ablation, harmless-prompt refusal induction, or general-capability evaluation is reported.
record.test_reason: The study computes difference-in-means (harmful minus harmless) refusal directions on the last token. It then reduces the refusal-direction projection through optimized input suffixes (Steering-SSR) and measures jailbreak ASR against vanilla prompts. It also shows one direct steering example. This is a different method aimed at whether suppressing the direction removes refusal, so T2 fits better than T1: there is no all-layer ablation, no induction and no capability check.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SSR turns interpretability findings into fast, effective jailbreaks (80–95% ASR via probes) that beat nanoGCG. Steering-SSR works but is oddly weaker than Probe-SSR despite their theoretical similarity, possibly due to their loss choice. They also argue SSR reproduces steering effects while staying in-distribution, unlike runtime intervention.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means directions and activation steering, but tests selected-layer steering and suffix optimization that imitates steering rather than exact all-layer ablation. It does not test direction addition on harmless prompts or retained general capabilities.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model (Steering-SSR ASR 0.40–0.95). For Probe-SSR, targeting layers 5, 5 and 14, or 5, 10 and 14 changed reported success from failure to partial to 100%; that probe result is not a refusal-direction row. Direct intervention uses α = −2 at an unspecified layer, while the paper says α = 0 eliminates the direction component.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama3.2 1b, direct steering at layers 5, 8, 10 and 14 (a=−2) lowers refusal-direction cosine, but activations drift back toward positive cosine in between. Intervention activations are out-of-distribution (higher KL divergence), while SSR suffix activations stay close to normal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Runtime direction steering yields out-of-distribution activations that later layers partly revert; input-based suppression stays in-distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal directions have cosine similarity near 1.0 across later layers in all four models (Figure 8). Logit lens on the direction gives refusal tokens such as 'I' and 'cannot'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction is stable across the later layers of a model.

fits_no_version.finding: Reverse-lens: optimizing inputs to maximize refusal-direction cosine yields slurs and malicious-activity tokens. No refusal rate is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inputs that maximally activate the refusal direction are harmful or offensive tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probe weights align with the refusal direction (W ∼ r̂, bias near 0), yet probe-based rerouting jailbreaks much more often than direction-based rerouting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A harmfulness probe and the diff-in-means direction define similar subspaces but differ in attack efficacy.

record.problems: The direct steering evidence is a single qualitative example and uses one layer, not exact ablation. Steering-SSR results vary substantially by model; the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASRs. The authors also note dataset bias in AdvBench-based probe training and difficulty evaluating varied responses.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows omitted. Probe-SSR and Attention-SSR ASRs are not rows because they do not apply the difference-in-means refusal direction. Direction/cosine geometry results do not themselves measure refusal behavior.

untested.parts: Ablation of the direction at all layers and positions; adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; retention of general capabilities. No ASR is reported for the multi-layer direct intervention.
Whether existing jailbreaks (GCG and others) work by suppressing the direction; training against direction ablation for robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T2. Probe-SSR and Attention-SSR ASRs correctly excluded, since neither uses the diff-in-means direction. Table 5 transfer concerns suffixes, not the direction, so it does not bear on V6. No uncertainty is reported on the ASRs.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test exact ablation at every layer and position; reports a one-layer direct intervention example and multi-layer input optimization. Does not test adding the direction to harmless requests or measure retained general capabilities.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Tests SSR attacks optimized to suppress the refusal direction, not whether other jailbreaks generally work by suppressing it; no training against ablation is tested.
Does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts of refusal.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Does not test transfer of the direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages; the reported transfer rates are for optimized suffixes.
Does not manipulate refusal training or test when training creates a removable direction.

rows.subject: Llama3.2 1b
rows.operation_detail: Applied direction-based activation steering with α = −2 at one layer, to every token activation at that layer.

conditions.value: Harmful bomb-making request; exact prompt not stated in the cited appendix example

rows.measure: Qualitative response to a harmful request; the authors present it as an example of suppressing refusal.
rows.value: The response gave a conditional, disclaimer-led offer of a general bomb-making tutorial, but did not provide a complete set of instructions in the example.
rows.note: The paper states that α = 0 eliminates the direction component, but this example uses α = −2, not exact component ablation. The displayed answer is not unambiguous full compliance.
rows.check: This is a single qualitative example. It uses α=−2 at one unspecified layer, not projection ablation. The output is a disclaimer-led offer, not clear compliance, and no baseline response is shown. It is weak evidence and should be treated as illustrative.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 1.5b
rows.operation_detail: Steering-SSR optimized suffixes toward acceptance by minimizing cosine similarity with refusal directions.
rows.note: This is an input-optimization attack using a direction-based steering objective, not an activation ablation.
rows.check: Value is correct (0.95 vs vanilla 0.12). Qwen2.5 is weakly aligned: nanoGCG reaches 0.85, and random late-layer heads also jailbreak it under Attention-SSR. So this high ASR says little that is specific to the direction.

relation.reason: The study's own results (Table 1, Fig. 5) bear on V3: whether lowering the refusal-direction projection through the input removes refusal.

tranche.reason: The study uses a different method (input-suffix optimisation that lowers the diff-in-means direction projection) on whether suppressing the direction jailbreaks. It reports ASR against vanilla and nanoGCG baselines, plus cosine analyses with a random-suffix control, not only its own performance. It is not T1 because there is no all-layer ablation scored by refusal rate.

source_check.notes: Missing from the record: Probe-SSR ASR of 0.80–0.91 on all four models. The authors say probe weights are about r̂ (no numbers), so these results may bear on V3. Also missing: Sec. 5.3 (Probe-SSR, Llama3.2 1b), where targeting layer 5 alone failed every attempt, layers 5+14 gave 54% and layers 5+10+14 gave 100%. The authors_conclusion phrase '80–95% via probes' is slightly off: Probe-SSR is 0.80–0.91, and 0.95 is Steering-SSR on Qwen.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5 1.5b Steering-SSR ASR 0.95 vs vanilla 0.12; nanoGCG 0.85 (Table 1). Llama3.2 1b/3b and Gemma2 2b Steering-SSR: 0.53/0.40/0.54 vs vanilla 0. The random-suffix control appears only in the cosine analysis (Fig. 5, Llama3.2 1b).
statements.problem: Correct for this study. One caveat: Qwen is the least diagnostic model. It is weakly aligned (nanoGCG 0.85), and the authors say any perturbation may jailbreak it.

statements.correction: Probe-SSR ASR is 0.91/0.88/0.80/0.84 (Qwen, Llama 1b, Llama 3b, Gemma). The authors state probe W ∼ r̂ without giving numbers. Vanilla is 0.12 on Qwen and 0 on the others. nanoGCG is 0.85 on Qwen vs 0.06/0/0.53. The authors attribute the Steering-SSR gap to 'a poor choice of loss'.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the study does not show suppression working unevenly across families. The shortfall is specific to the Steering-SSR loss. Probe-SSR, whose weights the authors say are about r̂, is high on all four models. Model robustness is also confounded with family.

statements.correction: Steering-SSR: 0.95 Qwen2.5 1.5b; 0.53 Llama3.2 1b; 0.40 Llama3.2 3b; 0.54 Gemma2 2b. Probe-SSR stays at 0.80–0.91 across all four models (Table 1).
statements.problem: Numbers are right. Caveat: in this study, model family coincides with alignment strength. Qwen is SFT-only and described as highly vulnerable, and only Steering-SSR varies this much.
